qs.q: To delete the first node in a single linked list, you would

c.x: Set the first link to None
Modify the first link to equal the link followed by the first one
Traverse the list until you reach None
Update the first link to a new node's reference

e: The lecture's remove_first(L) algorithm: if L.head is None the list is empty (error); otherwise L.head = L.head.next, then decrement the size.
So the head must be moved to the node that follows it (the next reference of the first node).
Setting head to None would delete the whole list, traversal is not needed, and a new node is not involved in a removal.

qs.q: Consider an example of an unsorted singly linked list in practice (assume only a reference to the head node is kept). Given the representation, which action can be carried out in $O(1)$ time?

c.x: Insertion at the middle of the linked list
Insertion at the end of the linked list
Deletion of the front node of the linked list
Deletion of the last node of the linked list

e: With only a head reference, deleting the front node needs just head = head.next: one step, $O(1)$.
Insertion at the middle needs a traversal to reach the position: $O(n)$.
Insertion at the end needs a traversal to find the last node (it is $O(1)$ only if an explicit tail reference is stored, which is not assumed here).
Deleting the last node of a singly linked list needs the node before it, and nodes have no previous reference, so it takes $O(n)$.

qs.q: Having two singly linked lists, list1 and list2. How would you efficiently concatenate them to produce a whole single list?

c.x: Set the last node link's next of list1 equal to the first node of list2.
Traverse list2; add one node to list1 at each iteration.
Traverse list1; add one node to list2 at each iteration.
Update the first link of list1 to reference the first link of list2.

e: Linking is only a reference update: list1.tail.next = list2.head, and the tail of the result becomes list2's tail.
This needs no copying of nodes, so it is very efficient (constant time with a tail reference).
Options 2 and 3 copy every node one by one ($O(n)$ work), and option 4 would make the first node of list1 point away and lose the rest of list1.

qs.q: Which of the following is a 'Linear' data structure?
e: A linked list is a linear data structure whose nodes form a single sequence, each node pointing to the next one.
Trees (hierarchical) and graphs (network) are non-linear structures, and a map stores key-value pairs rather than a sequence.

qs.q: In a Linked List, each node contains the data and a reference to the:
e: In a singly linked list each node holds an element and a next reference to the following node; the last node's next is None.
A previous reference exists only in doubly linked lists, and the root belongs to trees.

qs.q: A Python List is different from a standard Array because:

c.x: List is faster in all cases

e: One main disadvantage of arrays is fixed size: once allocated, the size cannot easily be increased or decreased.
A Python list grows dynamically (its underlying array is resized when full), so the difference is that a standard array has a fixed size.
Arrays are not dynamic, a list is not faster in all cases, and storage location is not the difference.

qs.q: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in an Array by its index?
e: Arrays use contiguous memory, so the address of any element is computed directly from its index: random access in $O(1)$.
The lecture's comparison: array access is $O(1)$ (random access), while a linked list needs $O(n)$ sequential access.
So 'accessing any element of an array takes $O(n)$' (2022 True/False) is False and 'accessing an array element is $O(1)$' (2024 True/False) is True.

qs.q: True or False: It is best to use an Array rather than a Linked List if I know the maximum number of items I need in advance.
e: The drawbacks of arrays are their fixed size (wasted memory if over-allocated, no growth if under-allocated).
If the maximum number of items is known in advance, these drawbacks disappear, and the array keeps its advantages: $O(1)$ random access and no per-node pointer overhead.
So the statement is True.

qs.q: True or False: A common shortcoming of using sequential (array-like) structures is that they force allocating chunks of contiguous free memory, which may be hard to find for large requests.
e: Arrays require contiguous memory blocks, and a very large array may be hard to fit in a single free block.
A linked list stores nodes in non-contiguous locations, allocated one by one, so it avoids this problem.
So the statement is True.

qs.q: True or False: If a singly linked list is not empty, updating only two links is required for the insert operation.
e: Insert at the head: newest.next = L.head, then L.head = newest. That is two reference updates.
Insert at the tail: L.tail.next = newest, then L.tail = newest. Again two updates.
No existing node needs to be moved, so the statement is True.

qs.q: True or False: Accessing an element of a single linked list may take up to $O(n \log n)$ in the worst case.
e: Access in a linked list is sequential: start at the head and follow next references.
In the worst case (the last element) this visits all n nodes, i.e. $O(n)$.
There is no sorting or logarithmic step involved, so $O(n \log n)$ is False.

qs.q: True or False: The last element of a single linked list always points to null (None).
e: The tail of a singly linked list is identified as the node whose next reference is None.
This is how traversal knows where to stop. (Only in a circularly linked list does the tail point back to the head.)

qs.q: True or False: A linked list is a fixed data structure.
e: A linked list does not have a predetermined fixed size: nodes are allocated one by one as needed and added or removed freely.
Fixed size is the problem of arrays, not of linked lists.

qs.q: True or False: An array structure is the building block of a linked list data structure.
e: The building block of a linked list is the node, which stores an element and a reference to the next node.
Linked lists are specifically used where arrays are inadequate: nodes live in non-contiguous memory, unlike an array's contiguous block.

qs.q: List ____ refers to the process of systematically visiting each node.
e: Accessing each element of the list one by one, starting at the head and following the next references, is called traversing the linked list.
Add and remove change the list, and search looks for a specific item (it uses traversal but is not the visiting process itself).

qs.q: A/An ____ is a linear data structure that can grow or shrink in size.
e: A linked list is linear and dynamic: it has no predetermined size and nodes are added or removed as needed.
An array is linear but has a fixed size; a tree and a graph are non-linear.

qs.q: True or False: One disadvantage of using arrays to store data is that arrays are static structures and therefore cannot be easily extended or reduced to fit the data set.
e: Fixed size is the first array disadvantage listed in the lecture: the size cannot easily be increased or decreased after allocation.
Over-allocating wastes memory and under-allocating cannot be fixed easily, so the statement is True.

qs.q: True or False: In a 1-D array, elements are stored in contiguous bytes of memory.
e: Arrays require contiguous memory blocks, which is exactly what allows $O(1)$ random access by index.
This contrasts with linked lists, whose nodes are placed in non-contiguous memory locations.

qs.q: True or False: The size of an array is not fixed.
e: Arrays have a fixed size: once allocated it cannot easily be increased or decreased.
So 'the size of an array is not fixed' is False.

qs.q: Figure (1) shows a singly linked list: head -> 93 -> 17 -> 77 -> 31 -> null, and a new node 26 referenced by `temp`. Step 1: the new node's next is set to point to node 93 (the old first node). Step 2: head is set to point to node 26. Which operation of a single linked list structure does Figure (1) describe?
e: The new node is linked in front of the old head (newest.next = L.head), then head is moved to it (L.head = newest).
These are exactly the steps of the lecture's add_first(L, e) algorithm.
addAtEnd would change the tail's next reference, search only reads nodes, and remove would bypass a node.

qs.q: Figure (2) shows a singly linked list head -> 54 -> 26 -> 93 -> 17 -> 77 -> 31 -> null, where a pointer named `current` starts at node 54 and moves one node at a time (26, 93, 17, 77, 31) until it reaches null. Figure (2) is an illustration of the single linked list ____ process.
e: Moving a pointer from the head along the next references until None is reached is traversing the list.
Nothing is inserted or removed, so it is not an addition, and is_empty only checks whether the head is None.
Initialization would only create an empty list.
